notes: An authored simulation of two fictional teammates using Considea’s human decision gates. Dialogue, candidates, assessments and acceptance are illustrative. No new live agent session, web research, implementation or user study was performed for this story. Private follow-ups are summarized between rounds; only example approved shared statements are shown.

steps.label: Two starting points
steps.title: “We already have a group chat.”
paragraphs: Alice and Bob have 24 hours to build a hackathon prototype. These opening statements represent the summaries each person would approve after a private interview.

dialogue.speaker: Alice
dialogue.text: I can handle Python and a small database. Last time we lost half the day connecting unfinished pieces, so I want something we can get working early. I am not the person to build a polished frontend. No model training or university-system integration.

dialogue.speaker: Bob
dialogue.text: I can build the JavaScript interface. In my course project, someone said the slides were done, but the charts were still on their laptop. We found out just before presenting. I want to fix that, but another to-do list is a hard sell. We already have a group chat.

dialogue.speaker: Considea
dialogue.text: You both want a small project, but you have not agreed on the problem. Alice is optimizing for a dependable build; Bob needs a reason a group would open it. Start with one breakdown you can actually demonstrate.

steps.outcome: Shared starting point: a student-team prototype, 24 hours, Python backend and JavaScript frontend. The product direction is still open.

steps.label: Name the real problem
steps.title: A missing owner—or an unfinished handoff?
paragraphs: Round 1 · The Negotiator asks whether the failure was assigning work or knowing when a teammate could use the result. The replies below are shared answers, not private interview transcripts.

dialogue.speaker: Alice
dialogue.text: My first thought was a board with a name and a deadline on each task. At least everyone would know who is doing what.

dialogue.speaker: Bob
dialogue.text: We knew who owned the slides. That was not the problem. “Done” meant one thing to the person making them and another to the person presenting. A board full of green checkboxes would have looked fine.

dialogue.speaker: Considea
dialogue.text: What would the presenter have needed to see before trusting that task was finished?

dialogue.speaker: Bob
dialogue.text: A link to the deck, the actual charts in it, and permission to open it. Not a message saying “nearly there.” I could check that without another meeting.

dialogue.speaker: Alice
dialogue.text: Okay, that is narrower than a task manager. We could put “what needs to be handed over” next to each task. I can build that. I do not want us promising that the app can judge whether the work is good.

steps.outcome: Focus on a handoff: the next person needs a usable deliverable, not just an assigned task. Quality judgment stays with the team.

steps.label: Cut the risky shortcut
steps.title: Would AI save time—or create more checking?
paragraphs: Round 2 · After another private follow-up and approved summary, Bob raises a practical objection: nobody wants to retype the group chat.

dialogue.speaker: Bob
dialogue.text: If we make everyone type tasks again, they will stay in the chat. Could we paste the conversation and have AI pull out the commitments?

dialogue.speaker: Alice
dialogue.text: Maybe, but “I can probably do the graphs” is not an assignment. We would need people to check owners and deadlines anyway. There is also chat content the group might not want to upload.

dialogue.speaker: Considea
dialogue.text: For tomorrow’s prototype, which matters more: importing a conversation or proving that a handoff is clearer? What is the smallest entry flow Bob would tolerate?

dialogue.speaker: Bob
dialogue.text: One person enters three agreed tasks at the end of the meeting. Task, owner, due time, and one sentence describing the handoff. No separate setup wizard. I still think entry effort could kill it, so we should test that.

dialogue.speaker: Alice
dialogue.text: That works. I can have create, edit and save working first. If manual entry is already too painful, adding an AI step will not prove this version is useful.

steps.outcome: Use manual entry for three agreed tasks. Defer chat import, AI extraction and notifications. Keep input effort as a testable concern, not a solved problem.

steps.label: Define “ready”
steps.title: “Done” still needs a shared meaning.
paragraphs: Round 3 · The scope is smaller, but a checkbox would recreate the original ambiguity. The team works through one concrete task.

dialogue.speaker: Considea
dialogue.text: Take “finish the charts.” What would its handoff condition say, and what would someone attach when they were ready?

dialogue.speaker: Bob
dialogue.text: “Put two labeled charts in the shared deck and make the deck viewable.” The person could paste the deck link when ready. Then I would know where to look.

dialogue.speaker: Alice
dialogue.text: A link field is easy. Verifying that the charts exist or that every teammate has permission is not. Also, a rehearsal or a spoken explanation might need a note instead of a link.

dialogue.speaker: Bob
dialogue.text: Fair. A link or a short note, and call the state “ready to hand over.” I was imagining the next person confirming receipt too, but that may be another whole workflow.

dialogue.speaker: Considea
dialogue.text: You have agreement on a visible handoff condition and a link or note. Recipient confirmation is still unresolved. The prototype must not label a link as verified just because it was supplied.

steps.outcome: A task needs an owner, due time, handoff condition and delivery note. “Ready” is a member’s statement. Recipient confirmation remains a decision for the candidate review.

steps.label: Agree to explore
steps.title: What can two people actually finish in 24 hours?
paragraphs: Round 4 · Considea checks the remaining constraints. Finishing this round opens the choice to generate; each member still has to choose.

dialogue.speaker: Alice
dialogue.text: I can own a small Python API with SQLite for the local demo. One board, seeded team names, no accounts. Let us agree on the task fields in the first hour and connect one saved task by hour six. I need time for integration, not just backend work.

dialogue.speaker: Bob
dialogue.text: I will own the mobile layout and task editing. Seeded names are okay for the demo, but we must not call that secure team access. I can aim to ask two classmates to try it. They have not agreed yet, so that is a plan, not user validation.

dialogue.speaker: Considea
dialogue.text: The build target is one local board with persistent tasks, not a deployed campus service. The test target is whether another person can find what to use next without asking in chat. Are you ready to compare candidate directions, or do you need another discussion?

dialogue.speaker: Alice
dialogue.text: Generate. My condition is that authentication, file storage and automatic link checks stay outside the prototype.

dialogue.speaker: Bob
dialogue.text: Generate. But show us an alternative to the board too. If it is just a task list with one extra field, I want the review to say that.

steps.outcome: Both members explicitly choose generation. Shared limits: one local board, 24 hours, no accounts or external integrations. Acceptance of a final project has not happened yet.

steps.label: Compare the options
steps.title: A useful direction, with one step too many.
paragraphs: Illustrative generator and evaluator outputs · These are authored examples of a plausible review, not results from a new model call or web search.

dialogue.speaker: Considea
dialogue.text: Three directions fit the discussion: Handoff Board makes deliverables visible; Meeting Closeout produces a copyable agreement after a meeting; Blocker Check-in asks what each person is waiting for. The board most directly addresses Bob’s missing-chart example.

dialogue.speaker: Bob
dialogue.text: Meeting Closeout is attractive because we can paste it into the chat. But once the meeting ends, it goes stale. I would choose the board if I can see the actual handoff in one glance.

dialogue.speaker: Alice
dialogue.text: The first board draft adds a recipient and a “confirm received” step. That means another person has to come back before a task moves on. I can code it, but I do not think we have shown that we need it.

dialogue.speaker: Bob
dialogue.text: I was the one who suggested confirmation. Looking at the flow, it is too much for tomorrow. Show the handoff condition beside the link or note and let the owner mark it ready. I can check it myself.

steps.outcome: They choose Handoff Board and both request a minor revision of version 1: remove recipient approval. The other directions are retained as alternatives, not silently merged into the scope.

candidate.title: Handoff Board · Version 1
candidate.problem: A teammate says a task is finished, but the next person cannot find or use the deliverable.
candidate.solution: One shared task board pairs a handoff condition with a delivery link or note. The first draft also asks a named recipient to confirm receipt.
mvp_scope: Task, owner, due time and a one-sentence handoff condition.
Delivery link or note; ready and received states.
One local board with persistent storage and a mobile-friendly view.
out_of_scope: Chat import, AI extraction, reminders and calendar sync.
Accounts, file uploads, permission checks and automatic quality judgments.

report.basis: Simulated assessment · no external evidence collected for this scenario.

novelty.reason: Owners, deadlines and checklists are familiar task-management patterns. Making handoff conditions prominent may be useful, but this scenario provides no comparative research or user evidence that establishes a distinct advantage.
missing_information: Compare the same handoff in a group chat, a shared document and this board.

feasibility.reason: A local single-board prototype is plausible given the stated skills. Recipient approval adds a second-person dependency; storage, integration and the 24-hour estimate have not been tested.
missing_information: Prove that a task and its ready state survive reload and a local server restart.
Check that the flow is usable on a phone before adding more states.

steps.label: Make the trade-off
steps.title: Less workflow. A clearer handoff.
paragraphs: The generator revises the same candidate. Version 2 gets its own assessment; the earlier decisions do not count as acceptance of this version.

dialogue.speaker: Considea
dialogue.text: Version 2 removes the recipient field and receipt approval. The owner marks a task ready after adding a delivery link or note. Anyone can read the handoff condition; the app does not verify the work. No new integrations were added.

dialogue.speaker: Alice
dialogue.text: For the demo, I will validate required fields on the server and save the ready state in SQLite. If the save fails, the interface must keep the draft and show an error. A green state that only exists in the browser would recreate the trust problem.

dialogue.speaker: Bob
dialogue.text: I will keep the condition and delivery note on the same card, including on a narrow phone screen. Also, can we call it “ready” everywhere? “Verified” would imply we checked the link, and we are explicitly not doing that.

dialogue.speaker: Considea
dialogue.text: The revision removes one dependency and makes failure handling explicit. The remaining uncertainty is usefulness: people can put an empty promise in a note too. Test whether the handoff condition changes what they actually share.

steps.outcome: Version 2 is ready for individual review. It is a smaller build with clearer acceptance checks; it is still an unbuilt, unvalidated proposal.

candidate.title: Handoff Board · Version 2
candidate.problem: A teammate says a task is finished, but the next person cannot find or use the deliverable.
candidate.solution: Before starting, agree what the next person needs. When ready, attach a link or note beside that condition. Keep the task and its state after refresh; leave judgment to the people using it.
mvp_scope: One board: task, owner, due time, handoff condition and delivery link or note.
Two states: in progress and ready to hand over. A delivery link or note is required before marking ready.
Create, edit and reopen tasks; persist changes in the local database.
One shared card layout on desktop and phone; preserve the draft when a save fails.
out_of_scope: Chat import, AI extraction, reminders and calendar sync.
Accounts, file uploads, permission checks and automatic quality judgments.
Recipient approval, automatic link checking and production access control.

report.basis: Simulated re-evaluation of version 2 · no build, user test or research run is claimed.

novelty.reason: Removing approval does not establish novelty. The hypothesis is that visible handoff conditions reduce clarification messages; only a comparison with the team’s current workflow can test that.
missing_information: Observe whether a receiver still needs to ask where the deliverable is or whether it is usable.

feasibility.reason: The scope is more manageable without a second-person approval flow. Feasibility remains an estimate until Alice and Bob connect the UI to persistence and run the agreed checks.
missing_information: Run create → mark ready → refresh → restart → reopen using the same stored task.

steps.label: Leave with a plan
steps.title: “I can own this version.”
paragraphs: Illustrative ending · Each person reviews candidate version 2 and its current assessment before accepting. The resulting brief records a decision to build, not a finished product.

dialogue.speaker: Alice
dialogue.text: I accept version 2 with the current assessment. I own the API, SQLite persistence and the restart check. If the first end-to-end task is not working by hour six, we stop adding features and fix that path.

dialogue.speaker: Bob
dialogue.text: I accept version 2 too. I own the interface, the mobile check and the test script. I will try to recruit two classmates. If nobody is available, we will label our own role-play as a rehearsal, not claim we tested it with users.

dialogue.speaker: Considea
dialogue.text: Both accept the same version. The brief includes the scope, owners, checkpoints and unresolved evidence. The team is aligned on what to try next; adoption and differentiation remain open.

steps.outcome: Expected result: an accepted version-2 brief for a 24-hour prototype, with explicit responsibilities and a way to discover that the idea is not useful enough.
deliverables: First hour · Agree the task fields, an example response and the handoff wording. Alice and Bob do this together.
By hour 6 · Alice and Bob connect one task from the interface to SQLite and reload it successfully. If blocked, pause feature work.
By hour 16 · Bob finishes the single-board flow; Alice checks edits, ready-state validation and failed saves. Keep the remaining time for integration and rehearsal.

Technical acceptance · Create a task, attach a delivery note, mark it ready, refresh, restart the local server and reopen the same task. Stored fields and state must match. Check the flow at 375px width.

Usefulness check · Give a receiver the three sample tasks. Can they find the deliverable and say what is ready without asking the author? Compare against the same information in a chat message. Record entry time and remaining questions; do not claim a statistical result from two people.
Decision after the test · If the chat is equally clear or the board takes too much work to maintain, revisit Meeting Closeout or stop. Shared agreement is permission to test, not evidence of demand.
